every compound-specific empirical claim in the supplied query prior or cited

claims.claim: Chrysin, a polyphenolic flavone, has measured oral bioavailability <1% in healthy volunteers (C02) and predicted absolute bioavailability 0.003–0.02% in humans (C16), demonstrating very low F for a related phenolic natural product.
Curcumin is consistently reported to have poor/low oral bioavailability in humans and rodents (C07, C13, C14, C19), supporting a low-F pattern for polyphenolic natural products.

Anthocyanin glycosides (peonidin and petunidin) show fractional bioavailability of only 0.14–0.48% in humans (C01, C03, C04, C05, C10, C11, C12, C17), and flavonolignans show very low oral bioavailability based on high apparent oral clearance (C18, C15, C08, C06, C09).

Scopoletin shares the phenolic and aromatic natural-product features of these low-F compounds; the high transfer likelihood of these contexts supports applying the low-F direction despite its smaller size and better solubility.

evidence_gaps: No direct scopoletin-specific oral bioavailability or pharmacokinetic record is available; prediction relies on transfer from related polyphenols.
Scopoletin's smaller size and better solubility than chrysin/curcumin/silybin could improve F, but the extent is unknown.
First-pass glucuronidation/sulfation of the phenolic OH is inferred, not directly measured for scopoletin.
content.decision_summary: The consistent very low oral bioavailability of structurally related polyphenolic natural products (chrysin, curcumin, anthocyanins, flavonolignans) and the high transfer likelihood of these contexts support F < 20% for scopoletin, despite favorable physicochemical priors.
